title: Race Conditions: Why count++ Isn't Safe
oneLiner: Interleave two threads' load, add and store yourself and watch an update vanish, then add a lock and try to break it again.
keyTakeaway: count++ is three steps: load the value into a register, add one, store it back. If another thread runs between the load and the store, both threads write the same result and one increment is lost. A race condition is any bug whose outcome depends on the timing of threads. The fix is to make the read-modify-write atomic (indivisible: no other thread can see it half done): a lock around it, or Interlocked.Increment for a single number.
explanation:
In C#, count++ looks like one operation, but the CPU sees three: LOAD the current value of count from memory into a register, ADD 1 to the register, STORE the register back to memory. Each thread has its own registers. If thread A loads 0, and before it stores, thread B also loads 0, then both compute 1 and both store 1. Two increments ran and count went up by one. This is a lost update, and it is the classic data race: two threads access the same memory, at least one of them writes, and nothing orders the accesses.

The nasty part is that it usually works. The two threads have to touch the counter within a window a few nanoseconds wide, so a test that increments a few hundred times may pass every run on your laptop, and then lose thousands of updates on a busy 32-core server. Races are timing dependent, which makes them hard to reproduce. You find them by reasoning about every possible interleaving, which is what the stepper below lets you do: you play the scheduler.

The fix is mutual exclusion. A critical section is code that touches shared state and must not run on two threads at once. Wrapping it in lock (gate) { count++; } means a thread must acquire the lock before the load and holds it until after the store; a second thread that reaches the lock blocks until the first releases it. The load, add and store now happen as one indivisible unit as far as every other thread using the same lock is concerned. Every access to the shared value must take the same lock: a lock only protects code that agrees to use it.

For a single integer, Interlocked.Increment(ref count) does the whole read-modify-write as one atomic CPU instruction (lock xadd on x86), with no lock object and no blocking. It is faster, but it only works for one variable; the moment an invariant (a rule that must always hold, like "the balance equals the sum of the history") spans two fields you need a lock. Check-then-act races are the same bug in another shape: if (!dict.ContainsKey(k)) dict[k] = v; can let two threads both see "missing" and both insert. Use ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd or a lock around the whole check-and-act.
